verdict: 2019+ QX50 with the 2.0L VC-Turbo and CVT is a new, complex design. RepairPal rates the QX50 line 4/5, but Edmunds criticizes the powertrain and repair-cost sites report internal engine failures. A 2021 with 186k miles is very unusual (likely fleet/rideshare) and is far past what most VC-Turbo engines have shown. Out-of-warranty electronics and the variable-compression mechanism are expensive.
major_issues: VC-Turbo variable-compression multilink and actuator wear (reported 50-90k mi; engine repair or replacement $5k-$9k). Nissan recall/service campaign for 2019-2022 VC-Turbo debris inspection and oil change. CVT cooler and CVT judder/cold-weather issues ($600-$1,500 service, $4k+ replacement). Turbo and boost leaks, infotainment and ProPilot sensor faults.
risk_reason: 186k miles on a first-generation VC-Turbo is beyond the data. Any engine or CVT fault is a multi-thousand dollar repair. Luxury parts and labor make even brakes, suspension and sensors expensive at this mileage.
inspect_today: Cold start and listen for rattle, knock or chain noise. Check oil level and condition (milky or metallic sparkle). Scan for codes and pending misfires. Confirm the VC-Turbo recall/service campaign was completed (VIN lookup). Check CVT fluid color and smell. During a drive, check for judder, slip and delayed engagement. Look for oil leaks at the turbo and valve cover. Check for coolant loss. Test ProPilot and cameras and the infotainment screen. Ask whether it was rideshare or fleet.

verdict: The 3.5L VQ35DE V6 is a solid engine, but the 2013-2015 CVT in the QX60 has a poor record: shudder, slip and failure. Many units were replaced or reprogrammed earlier, so an original unit at 187k is either lucky or already replaced. Rest of the vehicle is average.
major_issues: CVT failure (CarComplaints: avg $4,000 at ~59k mi; shudder $5,800 at ~121k mi; replacement $4,500-$8,000). CVT overheating and limp mode. Some 2013-2015 VINs had extended CVT coverage (120k/10yr), long expired at this mileage. Also oil gallery and oil cooler leaks, AC and compressor issues, and wheel bearings.
risk_reason: The CVT is the known weak point and the car has 187k miles. If original it is on borrowed time, and failure costs $4k-$8k. Even a healthy example probably needs brakes, suspension and other age-related work.
inspect_today: Cold start and check for CVT hesitation, shudder on light throttle at 20-45 mph, whine, and slip or RPM flare. Check CVT fluid condition and ask for proof of CVT replacement or fluid service. Scan for codes. Check engine oil leaks, and the AWD rear coupling and diff. Inspect for coolant mixing in the CVT cooler lines. Look at tires for uneven wear and check control arm bushings and wheel bearings. Test AC.

verdict: 2017 Compass (new MP generation) with the 2.4L Tigershark and ZF 9-speed or AWD driveline. Consumer Reports rates it below average, with a high complaint volume. The 2.4 has oil consumption problems and the transmission and driveline have a mixed record. Not a good fit for a low-repair budget at 181k.
major_issues: 2.4L Tigershark oil consumption (2017-18 Compass was in a class-action settlement; extended powertrain to 7yr/100k, now expired). Spun rod bearings and engine failure ($4k-$7k). ZF 9-speed harsh shifts, hesitation, software updates; failure $3.5k-$5k. 4WD rear drive unit and PTU wear and leaks ($1k-$2.5k). Electrical and infotainment glitches, stop-start issues, and recalls.
risk_reason: Known oil-burning engine, a transmission with a poor reputation, and a 4WD system with weak parts, all at 181k miles. Several of these are outside the budget when they fail.
inspect_today: Check oil level and color on the dipstick (low or sludgy suggests oil burning). Look for blue smoke on cold start and revving. Listen for rod knock. Scan for codes. During a drive check for harsh 1-2 and 2-3 shifts, hunting, and shudder. Check PTU and rear differential for leaks and whine. Check the stop-start function, backup camera and radio. Check for open recalls by VIN.

verdict: 2017 Cherokee KL with the 3.2L Pentastar V6, ZF 9-speed and 4WD (Active Drive I/II). The V6 itself is decent, but the 9-speed has a poor record and the PTU/rear unit on 4WD models is a known failure and recall item. Consumer-level reliability is below average.
major_issues: ZF 9-speed harsh or delayed shifts, shudder, and failures (rebuild or replacement $3.5k-$6k; commonly 60-130k mi). PTU failure on 4WD (about $1.5k-$2.5k; a recent PTU recall follows a crash). Pentastar rocker arm / valve train tick and cylinder head or cylinder #2 misfires at high mileage. Water pump and coolant leaks (~$600-$1,000). Oil cooler/filter housing leaks. Electrical and sensor faults.
risk_reason: At 182k miles a 9-speed and 4WD PTU are both likely to need work. Either one blows the budget. Even if the transmission is fine, cooling and valve train repairs are likely to exceed $1,000.
inspect_today: Check transmission fluid condition and run through all gears on a drive, watching for flare, harsh shifts and shudder at 40-60 mph. Check PTU and rear drive for leaks and whine (burnt gear oil smell). Listen for valve train tick and check for misfire codes. Check coolant level and water pump area for crusty residue. Inspect oil filter housing for leaks. Check for open PTU recall. Test all electronics and the 4WD indicator.

verdict: 2017 Grand Cherokee WK2 with 3.6L Pentastar and the well-proven 8-speed. This is the best powertrain in the batch. RepairPal rates the model 3.5/5 with about $666 per year. Consumer Reports rates it below average due to electrical, air suspension (if equipped) and other items. At 153k miles it is the lowest-mileage car of its class here.
major_issues: Pentastar rocker arm / lifter failure and cylinder head misfire (cylinder #2), typically 100-170k mi ($1.5k-$4k). Oil cooler/filter housing leaks and water pump leaks (~$600-$1,000). Electrical (TIPM, sensors), transfer case issues on 4WD, and leaking panoramic roof or air suspension if equipped. Brake and suspension wear is expected at this mileage.
risk_reason: The drivetrain is sound, and at 153k miles it is the lowest mileage here. Still, water pump, oil cooler and valve train problems are common around this age, and the 4WD adds transfer case and suspension costs. Roughly a coin flip for one $1,000+ item.
inspect_today: Listen to a cold start for ticking (rocker arms) and check for misfire codes. Check oil filter housing and cooler area, and the water pump area for coolant residue. Check coolant level. Verify the 8-speed shifts smoothly at all speeds. Test the transfer case (4WD engagement) and look for front axle or driveshaft play. If it has air suspension, check ride height and look for sagging. Check the electronics, Uconnect and panoramic roof drains.

verdict: 2015 was the first Renegade year, with the most complaints, in particular about the ZF 9-speed. The 2.4L Tigershark also has an oil consumption record. At 188k miles the car is old, small, and likely to have had a hard life.
major_issues: ZF 9-speed harsh shifting, hesitation, and failure (CarComplaints: avg mileage ~14k, reflashed by the dealer; replacement $3.5k-$5k). 2.4L Tigershark oil consumption and rod bearing failure. PTU and rear drive unit failures on 4WD ($1k-$2.5k). Electrical faults, Uconnect and window regulators. Early-model recalls.
risk_reason: Weak first-year 9-speed, oil-burning 2.4L, and 4WD unit all at 188k miles. Any one is a 1,000+ dollar failure and there are several chances.
inspect_today: Check oil level and condition and look for oil burning smoke. Listen for rod knock. Scan codes. Drive for harsh 1-2 and 2-3 shifts, delayed engagement into drive or reverse, and shudder. Check PTU and rear unit for leaks. Test the 4WD selector (Select-Terrain). Check coolant and the sunroof and electronics. Verify recall completion by VIN.

verdict: 2015 Sorento (UM) with the 3.3L Lambda II GDI V6 and a conventional 6-speed automatic. RepairPal rates it 4/5 and ranks it 12th of 26. Consumer Reports rates it below average. The V6 and 6-speed are fairly durable, and it avoids the Theta II engine failures of the 2.4L. At 147k miles it is a reasonable choice in this batch.
major_issues: 3.3 GDI carbon buildup and misfires or rough idle (~$300-$900 cleaning). Valve cover and oil leaks, and water pump or coolant leaks (~$500-$900). Rear differential/transfer case wear on AWD. AC compressor, wheel bearings and suspension components. Check engine light from sensor and EVAP faults. Some recalls (3 per NHTSA).
risk_reason: The V6 and 6-speed have a decent record, but 147k miles on an as-is car with unknown maintenance means a decent chance of a water pump, AWD or suspension bill over $1,000. Lower than the Jeeps and Infinitis.
inspect_today: Check for oil leaks at valve covers and timing cover. Check oil level and condition. Scan for misfire and EVAP codes. Look for coolant residue at the water pump. Drive for smooth 6-speed shifting and AWD binding on tight turns. Check wheel bearings, struts and tire wear. Test AC. Check recall status by VIN.

verdict: 2016 Soul with the 1.6L Gamma GDI and 6-speed (auto or manual). Cheap parts and simple mechanicals, with RepairPal rating of 4 to 4.5/5. At 102k miles it is the lowest mileage in the batch. The main risk is the 1.6 GDI engine (oil consumption, ~100k mi failures), which CarComplaints lists for 2014-2016 Souls.
major_issues: 1.6L GDI engine failure or heavy oil consumption (CarComplaints: avg $7,000 at ~100k mi; oil use at ~97k mi). Catalytic converter and exhaust problems. Kia recall on engine and catalyst heat. Minor items: wheel bearings, AC, and audio or nav faults. Engine problems are most relevant if oil was neglected.
risk_reason: Low mileage for the batch, cheap parts, and a simple drivetrain. The main exposure is the 1.6 GDI engine at about 100k miles, but most Souls do not fail. Still, an engine problem would end the budget, so verify oil use before bidding.
inspect_today: Check oil level and condition, and for blue smoke on cold start and rev. Look for rod knock or ticking. Scan for codes and check the catalytic converter area. Look for service history or oil change records. Check coolant level. Drive for smooth shifts, wheel bearing hum and brake wear. Verify engine recall/warranty status by VIN.
